The depth-first search splits the edges into two chains, each a closed loop: A, C, B back to A (accent) and D, F, E back to D (teal). The bridge C–D, faded, lies on no cycle and so belongs to no chain. The card lists both chains as edge pairs in traversal order." width="100%"} A depth-first search splits the edges into tree edges and back edges. Each back edge starts a *chain*: the back edge followed by tree edges climbing towards the root until reaching a node already covered by an earlier chain. The chains cover every edge that lies on a cycle, and nothing else, so the edges left out are exactly the bridges. The first chain of each component is a cycle; later chains are cycles or paths that hang off earlier chains, like the "ears" of an ear decomposition. Chain decompositions give simple linear-time tests for 2-edge- and 2-vertex-connectivity and show how a network's cycles are layered. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [root]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str, None]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional start node (ID or label). If given, only its connected component is decomposed. If `None` (default), every component is, starting from the lowest node ID. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[tuple[int, int]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The chains, each a list of `(u, v)` node ID pairs in traversal order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or `root` does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Schmidt (2013) orients tree edges towards the root and back edges away from it, then visits the nodes in DFS preorder and, for each back edge leaving the current node, follows parent pointers until a visited node is reached. It runs in $O(V + E)$ time. The DFS visits neighbors in the order their edges were added and treats parallel edges as one, so the chains are identical to NetworkX's `chain_decomposition` for the same graph. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two triangles joined by a bridge decompose into two chains (one per triangle); the bridge C-D belongs to no chain: ::: {#e37ae6a1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) g.add_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D")] ) [ [(g.get_label_from_id(u), g.get_label_from_id(v)) for u, v in chain] for chain in g.chain_decomposition() ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [[('A', 'C'), ('C', 'B'), ('B', 'A')], [('D', 'F'), ('F', 'E'), ('E', 'D')]] ``` ::: :::
